solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Measure water supply first, and step lively!

indicators.note: first says the water supply piece comes ahead of the measure

parts.note: a tap is where water is drawn from the mains
a measure is an old word for a dance, especially a stately one

explanation.surface: A plumber's instruction: check the water supply first, then get moving smartly.
explanation.definitionFit: To dance with rhythmic clicking steps is a lively way of stepping, hence the exclamatory imperative.

clue.text: It's possibly an energy drink like tea

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters may be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the contraction, without the apostrophe
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Perhaps this is an energy drink that resembles tea.
explanation.definitionFit: An infusion of herbs or flowers is brewed and drunk much as tea is, a herbal tea.

clue.text: Digital V gesture that's not at all offensive

definitions.text: Digital V gesture that's not at all offensive

parts.words: Digital V gesture that's not at all offensive
parts.note: two raised fingers palm outward signal harmony, unlike the rude palm-inward version

explanation.surface: A note on hand signals: a V made with the fingers that causes no offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' means made with the fingers (digits), not electronic; 'offensive' also hints at military attack, the opposite of the gesture's message.
explanation.definitionFit: A V of two fingers held up palm outward is the well-known symbol for harmony and no war.

clue.text: A good number try to go topless

indicators.note: losing the top letter, since in a down entry the first letter sits at the top

parts.note: to sample something is to try it

explanation.surface: A cheeky dare: plenty of people attempt to strip off their tops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' is the deletion signal: drop the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful or more than enough, as a good number is.

clue.text: 2s in fuzzy close-up

indicators.note: fuzzy, as in blurred, signals the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Pairs appear in a blurred photograph taken at short range.
explanation.definitionFit: Pairs are twos, so the figure 2s stands for sets of two.

clue.text: They are widely known to be forgers

definitions.text: They are widely known to be forgers

parts.words: They are widely known to be forgers
parts.note: metalworkers forge iron at an anvil, and their trade name is also the commonest English surname, so it is known far and wide

explanation.surface: A notorious gang of counterfeiters whose reputation has spread far and wide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forgers' suggests fraudsters, but here it is people who hammer hot metal; 'widely known' plays on the surname being so common.
explanation.definitionFit: Blacksmiths and goldsmiths work metal at a forge, and the name is the most widespread English family name.

clue.text: Fat horse fed with special grain

indicators.note: fed with says the horse word takes the next piece inside it

parts.note: a mare is a female horse

indicators.note: special suggests the letters are made into something different

explanation.surface: A plump horse that has been given a particular kind of grain.
explanation.definitionFit: A butter substitute made from vegetable oils is an edible fat used for spreading and cooking.

clue.text: It goes up on the tenth

indicators.note: on means placed above in a down clue, so the reversed piece comes first
in a down entry going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word is reversed

explanation.surface: Something rises on the tenth day of the month.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce or income paid to support the church.

clue.text: Kick out the competition? You couldn't in this!

parts.note: to sack someone is to kick them out of a job
a race is a contest

explanation.surface: Eliminate your rivals? Impossible when your legs are tied up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kick out' also means a leg kick, which a competitor bagged up to the waist cannot manage.
explanation.definitionFit: In a hopping race inside a bag you cannot kick your legs at all, so the event fits the exclamation.

clue.text: Scotch and beer may ensnare a politician

indicators.note: to ensnare is to trap, so the beer word holds the following pieces inside it

parts.note: stout is a dark beer
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A drinker's tale: whisky and ale might be used to trap a member of parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour or plan is to crush it firmly, the same as to extinguish it completely.

clue.text: One quick-on-the-flaw, you might say

parts.note: a pun on 'quick on the draw': someone fast to spot faults in a work of art

explanation.surface: A gunslinger joke, with 'draw' twisted into 'flaw'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You might say' flags the wordplay on the cowboy phrase rather than a sound change.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer's job is to point out faults, so a sharp reviewer pounces on every flaw.

clue.text: Bishop is free of an extra responsibility

indicators.note: free of means without, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a bonus is an extra payment
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A clergyman is relieved of an additional duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The burden of a duty lies with whoever is accountable, a Latin word for burden.

clue.text: Female relative returning from Greece incognito

indicators.note: returning says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A woman of the family comes home from a secret trip to Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a female family member, the counterpart of a nephew.

clue.text: Pay attention to make an organ donation

definitions.meaning: read literally: give away, on loan, one of your hearing organs

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to listen, while its literal reading is lending out a body part, an organ.

clue.text: Last sign of cooked food outside rescue centre

indicators.note: outside says the food word wraps around the next piece

parts.note: pies are baked food

indicators.note: centre picks the two middle letters of the word rescue

explanation.surface: A notice at an animal shelter: the final clue that dinner was being cooked out back.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fishes are the twelfth and final sign of the zodiac in its usual order.

clue.text: Tragic French and English mix-up we've been warned about

indicators.note: a mix-up shuffles the letters together

parts.note: et is French for and

explanation.surface: A tragic Anglo-French muddle that someone cautioned us about.
explanation.definitionFit: Smoking carries government health warnings printed on every packet, so it is the thing we were cautioned against.

clue.text: Hugely significant size Mick is said to be

indicators.note: said tells us the words are heard, not spelt

parts.note: the phrase 'size Mick' spoken quickly

explanation.surface: Gossip about how big a man called Mick is reputed to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally relating to earthquakes, it is used figuratively for an event of enormous consequence.

clue.text: Accident caused by careless mechanics

indicators.note: careless suggests the letters are handled sloppily and come out rearranged

explanation.surface: A crash blamed on sloppy garage workers.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap or piece of bad luck is an unlucky event, much like an accident.

clue.text: Half-wrecked about a short mile off port

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters wrap the next pieces
wrecked says the letters of half are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for mile
out, as in a light that is off

explanation.surface: A ship lies partly wrecked just under a mile out from harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: FALMOUTH is a harbour town in Cornwall, south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cornish harbour town on one of the world's largest natural harbours is a port.

clue.text: After dark a drunk needs direction

indicators.note: needs here means takes in, so the drunk word holds the direction inside

parts.note: tight is slang for drunk
N is north, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A tipsy reveller stumbling home in the dark needs someone to point the way.
explanation.definitionFit: Once darkness falls it is night-time, so both phrases mean during the hours of darkness.

clue.text: There's a danger in role reversal

indicators.note: reversal says the word is turned back to front

parts.note: an actor's part is their role

explanation.surface: Swapping roles carries a risk.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare or pitfall is a hidden hazard, so a danger.

clue.text: Endless vast ocean featuring in a musical

indicators.note: endless says each of the two words loses its final letter

parts.note: a great sea is a vast ocean

explanation.surface: A boundless sea forms the backdrop in a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1971 stage show, later a 1978 film, set at Rydell High is a famous rock-and-roll musical.

clue.text: To retaliate, score any double

parts.note: to score is to get, as in getting a goal
doubling any whole number gives an even number

explanation.surface: Advice on revenge in a game: to strike back, hit any double.
explanation.definitionFit: Repaying an injury in kind settles the score, an idiom for taking revenge.

clue.text: He's over-ostentatious yet friendly

indicators.note: over means placed above in a down entry, so this piece comes first

parts.note: the pronoun he, the 's being is
arty can mean showily or pretentiously artistic

explanation.surface: A man who is overly showy, but warm all the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearty greeting is warm and cordial, a synonym for friendly.

clue.text: Shaw's Barbara definitely plays one

parts.note: Major Barbara is a George Bernard Shaw play whose title heroine has the leading role

explanation.surface: A theatre note about the star of a Shaw play.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's play Major Barbara the title character holds a Salvation Army rank, Major, so she 'definitely' has that role in both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The leading or principal role in a play is its biggest one, which the title heroine plays.

clue.text: Traitor just half sorry to be retiring

indicators.note: half takes the first two letters of the four-letter word
retiring means going back, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: sorry can mean sad or regretful

explanation.surface: A betrayer, only half regretful, is about to step down.
explanation.definitionFit: The disciple who betrayed Jesus for silver is the archetypal betrayer, so his name means a traitor.

clue.text: Colour regularly found among coach-horses

indicators.note: regularly picks every second letter of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A particular coat colour turns up often among horses that pull coaches.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowish-brown earth pigment, and the shade named after it.

clue.text: Outstanding old part of mansion

parts.note: a wing is a section of a large house

explanation.surface: A notable old section of a stately home.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt still to be paid is due, the sense in which money is still owed.

clue.text: At university a meeting can be brief

parts.note: to be up is to be in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge
a date is an arranged meeting

explanation.surface: A student tip: an appointment on campus can be kept short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' is a verb here, to inform someone of the latest news, not the adjective it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring someone up to date with the latest information is to brief them.

clue.text: Fine fare for a couch-potato?

parts.note: a ready meal eaten in front of the television is ideal food for someone who lounges on the sofa

explanation.surface: Wondering what makes a good meal for a lazy sofa-dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-packaged meal heated and eaten while watching the box is exactly what a sofa-bound viewer wants.

clue.text: Race held in Athens, maybe

indicators.note: maybe signals that the letters of the city name could be another word if rearranged

explanation.surface: A running event staged in the Greek capital, perhaps the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a noun for the athletic contest but is the verb, to hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: To race is to rush or hurry along, a verb synonym.

clue.text: German spy finally tracks weapons back to the bar-parlour

indicators.note: tracks means follows, so the German and spy pieces come after the weapons
back says the weapons word is written in reverse order

parts.note: guns are weapons

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of spy

explanation.surface: A thriller scene: a German agent traces an arms cache to a pub's back room.
explanation.walkthrough: A small cosy room in a pub, often called the snug, is a fairly old-fashioned British term.
explanation.definitionFit: A small comfortable private room in a pub or inn, a bar-parlour, is a cosy retreat by another name.
